items.followUp: Explain how pH and enzyme concentration affect the rate of enzyme action.

rubric.why: Low temperature slows molecular movement and enzyme activity.
rubric.description: States the effect of low temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that low temperature slows enzyme action.

rubric.why: As temperature rises, enzyme activity increases to a maximum at the optimum temperature.
rubric.description: States the effect of rising temperature up to the optimum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that activity increases to a maximum at the optimum temperature.

rubric.why: Above the optimum temperature, the enzyme is denatured and its active site changes shape.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of excessive temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that high temperature denatures the enzyme or changes its active site.

rubric.why: Increasing substrate concentration raises the rate until the enzyme's active sites are occupied and the rate levels off.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of substrate concentration, including saturation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the increase in rate and its levelling off when active sites are occupied.

modelAnswer: At low temperatures, enzyme activity is slow because molecules move more slowly.
As temperature rises, enzyme activity increases until it reaches a maximum at the enzyme's optimum temperature.
Above the optimum temperature, the enzyme is denatured; its active site changes shape and its activity falls.
Increasing substrate concentration increases the reaction rate while more substrate can bind to enzyme active sites.
The rate eventually levels off when all active sites are occupied.

items.followUp: Describe the role of ATP and NADPH in the Calvin cycle.

rubric.why: The dark reactions are associated with the work of Melvin Calvin.
rubric.description: Names the discoverer of the dark reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming Melvin Calvin.

rubric.why: The dark reactions take place in the chloroplast stroma.
rubric.description: States where the dark reactions occur.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the stroma of the chloroplast.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is fixed by combining with RuBP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that carbon dioxide combines with RuBP.

rubric.why: ATP and NADPH provide energy and reducing power for the conversion of PGA to PGAL.
rubric.description: Describes the reduction of PGA to PGAL.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ATP and NADPH are used to form PGAL from PGA.

rubric.why: PGAL contributes to sugar formation, and some is used to regenerate RuBP so the cycle can continue.
rubric.description: States the fate of PGAL and the regeneration step.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that PGAL forms sugars and/or is used to regenerate RuBP.

modelAnswer: The dark reactions were worked out by Melvin Calvin and are also called the Calvin cycle.
They occur in the stroma of chloroplasts and use ATP and NADPH made during the light reactions.
Carbon dioxide combines with RuBP (ribulose bisphosphate) and is fixed into an intermediate that forms PGA.
ATP and NADPH are used to reduce PGA to PGAL.
Some PGAL is used to make sugars, while the rest regenerates RuBP so the cycle can continue.

items.followUp: How did Ronald Ross provide evidence that mosquitoes transmit malaria?

rubric.why: King observed that malaria and mosquitoes occurred in the same places, and malaria was uncommon where mosquitoes were absent.
rubric.description: States the association between malaria and mosquitoes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the occurrence of malaria with the presence or distribution of mosquitoes.

rubric.why: His observations also linked malaria with seasonal mosquito abundance or protection from mosquitoes.
rubric.description: Gives another relevant observation by King.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant observation, such as malaria increasing when mosquitoes were plentiful or mosquito nets offering protection.

modelAnswer: A. F. A. King observed that malaria was common in places where mosquitoes were abundant and was uncommon where mosquitoes were absent.
He noted that malaria increased in the rainy season, when mosquitoes were plentiful, and that mosquito nets could help protect people from the disease.
